claims.text: The untreated high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous microstructure without distinct lubricious intergranular phases.
Adding approximately 10 at.% Ag and applying a controlled aging treatment will cause Ag to segregate to grain boundaries.
The Ag addition and aging treatment will form well-dispersed nanometric Ag-rich precipitates at grain boundaries.
During aging, grain-boundary Ag nucleates into a separate phase.
The Ag-rich precipitates have low shear strength.
The Ag-rich precipitates produce self-healing lubricious films.
The Ag-rich films provide a stable sliding interface at moving contact surfaces.
The stable, low-shear Ag-rich sliding interface reduces coefficient of friction.
The stable, low-shear Ag-rich sliding interface reduces wear rate.
Ag's inherent stability and ability to form a continuous lubricating layer make the mechanism effective across a range of temperatures.
The treatment is expected to remain effective from ambient to moderately high service temperatures if aging reliably forms the targeted precipitates and does not impair strength.
Compared under identical operating conditions, Ag addition plus aging will reduce coefficient of friction by approximately 30–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
Compared under identical operating conditions, Ag addition plus aging will reduce wear rate by approximately 30–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
Mechanical integrity and avoidance of unfavorable phase transformations are boundary conditions for the proposed service window.
